title: Risk-neutral probabilities
objectives: Derive risk-neutral probabilities and price by discounted expectation.
Explain why $q$ is a pricing weight and not a forecast.

screens.title: One weight
screens.prose: The call pays £20 or £0, and its copy costs £11.90. Look for one weight $q$ on the up state, with $1 - q$ on the down state, that reproduces the price.
screens.question: Which weight on up gives the copy’s price, £11.90?

hints.text: Move $q$ until the point meets the dashed line.
The dashed line is the copy’s cost.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the weight where the curve crosses the dashed line.

byKey.half: That is where the slider started. It gives £9.52, below the copy’s cost.
byKey.no-discount: You solved $20q = 11.90$ without discounting. The £20 arrives in a year, so divide by 1.05 first.

explain.text: At $q = 0.625$: $0.625 \times 20 / 1.05 = \text{£}11.90$, the copy’s cost. So the price is a discounted weighted average of the payoffs. Is 0.625 a chance, though?

screens.title: The same weight on the share
screens.prose: Put the weight $q = 0.625$ on the share’s own prices, £120 and £80. We write $E_q[S_1] = qS_u + (1 - q)S_d$ for the share’s expected price under $q$.
screens.question: What is $E_q[S_1]$?

hints.text: Weight each price by its branch.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two prices, each times its weight.

byKey.today: You took today’s price. Weight the two prices in a year instead.
byKey.up-only: You left out the down state. Add $0.375 \times 80 = 30$.

explain.text: $0.625 \times 120 + 0.375 \times 80 = 105$, which is £100 grown at 5%. Under $q$ the share earns the risk-free rate on average. That is why $q$ is called a **risk-neutral probability**.

screens.title: The weight on a new tree
screens.prose: A share costs £50 and ends at £55 or £45. The risk-free rate is 2%. Find the weight $q$ under which the share grows at the risk-free rate.
screens.question: What is $q$?

hints.text: Under $q$ the expected price is £50 grown at 2%.

byKey.half: With 0.5 the share grows to £50 on average, not £51. Lean the weight towards up.
byKey.swapped: That is $1 - q$, the weight on down.
byKey.rate: That is the rate. Use it to set the target, £51, then solve for $q$.

explain.text: Solve $55q + 45(1 - q) = 51$: $10q = 6$, so $q = 0.6$. In factors, $q = (1.02 - 0.9)/(1.1 - 0.9)$. No forecast went in, only prices and the rate.

screens.title: Pricing with the weights
screens.prose: Same tree, with $q = 0.6$. A call struck at £50 pays £5 if the share ends at £55 and £0 at £45.
screens.question: Price the call with $q$.

hints.text: Weight the payoffs, then discount one year.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the payoffs by $q$ and $1 - q$, then divide by 1.02.

byKey.no-discount: You forgot to discount. The £3 is an average payoff in a year; divide by 1.02.
byKey.half: You weighted the states 50/50. Use $q = 0.6$, the weight that makes the share earn 2%.
byKey.payoff: That is the most the call can pay, in a year. Weight it and discount it.

explain.text: $0.6 \times 5 / 1.02 = \text{£}2.94$. The copy agrees: $\Delta = 5/10 = 0.5$, borrow $22.50/1.02 = \text{£}22.06$, cost $25 - 22.06 = 2.94$. The weights are a shortcut for the copy.

screens.title: At the boundary
screens.prose: Back to £100 with $d = 0.8$ and $r = 5\%$. Now the up factor shrinks to $u = 1.05$, the same growth as lending.
screens.question: What is $q$ now?

hints.text: Use $q = \frac{(1 + r) - d}{u - d}$ with the new $u$.
Here $1 + r$ and $u$ are both 1.05.

feedback.correct: $q = 1$: all the weight sits on up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $u = 1.05$ into the formula.

byKey.old: That is $q$ for $u = 1.2$. The up factor is now 1.05.
byKey.zero: You put the weight on the wrong state. The top of the fraction is $1.05 - 0.8$, not zero.

explain.text: $q = 1$: the share can grow at 5% on average only if it surely goes up. That is the arbitrage boundary from lesson 1. Any $u$ below 1.05 gives $q > 1$; a weight outside 0 to 1 signals an arbitrage.

screens.title: Where the weight comes from
screens.prose: Start from the copy and rewrite its cost. Write $S_u = uS_0$, $S_d = dS_0$, and $c_u$, $c_d$ for the option’s payoffs.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $\Delta S_0 u + (1 + r)B = c_u$ and $\Delta S_0 d + (1 + r)B = c_d$: the copy pays the option in each state
$\Delta S_0 = \dfrac{c_u - c_d}{u - d}$ and $(1 + r)B = \dfrac{u c_d - d c_u}{u - d}$: solve the two equations
$c_0 = \Delta S_0 + B = \dfrac{(1 + r)(c_u - c_d) + u c_d - d c_u}{(1 + r)(u - d)}$: add, over one denominator
$c_0 = \dfrac{1}{1 + r}\left[\dfrac{(1 + r) - d}{u - d}\,c_u + \dfrac{u - (1 + r)}{u - d}\,c_d\right]$: collect the $c_u$ and $c_d$ terms
$c_0 = \dfrac{q\,c_u + (1 - q)\,c_d}{1 + r}$ with $q = \dfrac{(1 + r) - d}{u - d}$: the two weights add to 1

hints.text: Begin where lesson 2 began: one equation per state.
Solving gives $\Delta$ and $B$; only then can you add them.
Equations, solve, add, collect, then name the weights.

feedback.correct: The copy’s cost is a discounted weighted average, with weights $q$ and $1 - q$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line rewrites the one before it.

byKey.e: Naming $q$ needs the collected form first, so it comes last.
byKey.c: Adding needs $\Delta S_0$ and $B$ first, so it follows the solving line.

explain.text: The weight on $c_u$ is $\frac{(1 + r) - d}{u - d}$ and the weight on $c_d$ is $\frac{u - (1 + r)}{u - d}$. They add to $\frac{u - d}{u - d} = 1$. With $u = 1.2$, $d = 0.8$ and $r = 0.05$, $q = 0.25/0.4 = 0.625$.

screens.title: A name, not a belief
screens.prose: You priced with weights that make the share earn the risk-free rate: $$c_0 = \frac{q\,c_u + (1 - q)\,c_d}{1 + r}, \qquad q = \frac{(1 + r) - d}{u - d}.$$ Risk-neutral names the weights, not the investors.
screens.question: What is $q = 0.625$?

options.text: The weight under which the share grows at the risk-free rate
The market’s forecast that the share rises
options.why: You read $q$ as a belief. It came from £120, £80 and 5% alone; no forecast went in.
You took the name literally. The price came from copying, which works whatever investors feel about risk.

options.text: The real chance, adjusted for interest
options.why: No real chance entered the formula. Change the real chance and $q$ stays at 0.625.

hints.text: What went into the formula for $q$?
Only $u$, $d$ and $r$. So $q$ cannot be anyone’s forecast.

feedback.correct: $q$ is the weight that makes $E_q[S_1] = (1 + r)S_0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the formula for $q$ uses.

explain.text: $q$ is built from $u$, $d$ and $r$, so it is a pricing weight, not a forecast. It is the weight that makes $E_q[S_1] = (1 + r)S_0$. Real investors can hate risk and the price is still £11.90.

screens.title: A put, and a check
screens.prose: A put struck at £100 on the same tree pays £0 if up and £20 if down. A call minus a put pays $S_1 - 100$ in both states, so $c - p = S_0 - K/(1 + r)$.

state.caption: The call on this tree costs £11.90

screens.question: Price the put by $q$, then check the relation.

hints.text: Weight the put’s payoffs by $q$ and $1 - q$, then discount.
The put pays only in the down state, weight 0.375.

feedback.correct: £7.14, and both sides of the check give £4.76.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Price the put, then compute each side of the relation.

byKey.r0c1: The put pays £20 in the down state, weight $1 - q = 0.375$: $0.375 \times 20 / 1.05$.
byKey.r1c1: Subtract your put price from the call’s £11.90.

explain.text: $p = 0.375 \times 20 / 1.05 = \text{£}7.14$, the price you found by copying in lesson 2. Then $11.90 - 7.14 = 4.76 = 100 - 95.24$: **put-call parity** holds. One $q$ prices every payoff on the tree.

ideas: The copy’s cost can be rewritten as a discounted weighted average of the payoffs, with weights $q$ and $1 - q$.
$q$ is the weight under which the share grows at the risk-free rate: $E_q[S_1] = (1 + r)S_0$.
$q$ uses only $u$, $d$ and $r$. It lies in $(0, 1)$ exactly when there is no arbitrage.

formula.name: Risk-neutral pricing
formula.tex: c_0 = \dfrac{q\,c_u + (1 - q)\,c_d}{1 + r}, \quad q = \dfrac{(1 + r) - d}{u - d}
formula.note: Risk-neutral is a name for the weights, not an assumption about investors.

summary.trap: The real chance of up does not price the option. Using it, or reading $q$ as a forecast, gives a price someone can arbitrage.

explain.text: The digital pays £1 with weight $q$ and nothing otherwise: $0.625 \times 1 / 1.05 = \text{£}0.595$. A digital’s price is the discounted risk-neutral probability of its event.
